paras: The threatened lynching of Oscar Fifer took place at Athens, Tennessee, on February 25, 1888, when a crowd of Black residents surrounded the jail holding Fifer, a white man, hours after he shot and killed Matt Whiteside, described as a mulatto. According to a Chattanooga dispatch, the crowd said it would lynch Fifer before morning, but no report of what followed appears in the coverage. The story reached readers mainly through a brief wire item in Richmond and Savannah papers.
Fifer and Whiteside had an "old quarrel," which they renewed at Athens on the afternoon of February 25. The dispatch, which names no source, said Whiteside "assaulted the former with a knife."

Fifer then drew a revolver and shot Whiteside, killing him instantly. A separate news paragraph added that the bullet passed completely through Whiteside's body and struck a man named Brown, who was standing fifty feet away, wounding him seriously in the breast. Fifer was confined in the jail, and "Negroes" surrounded it, saying they would lynch him before morning.

The coverage does not show whether the crowd tried to take Fifer from the jail, how it dispersed, or whether he was later tried for Whiteside's death. No report of an inquest into Whiteside's death or of Brown's recovery was found.

The Chattanooga telegram ran on February 26 in the Richmond Dispatch under the headline "Fatal Affray in Tennessee" and in the Savannah Morning News under "Negroes Surround a Jail." Both printings labeled Fifer "white" and Whiteside a "mulatto" and gave the knife assault as fact, though they differed on the wound, Richmond printing "through the head" and Savannah "through the heart." The Savannah headline made the Black crowd, rather than the killing, the point of the story.

A different version circulated as a short item among miscellany, appearing in the New York Evening World on February 29 and the Washington Evening Star on March 2. That paragraph gave no races and said nothing of the jail or the threat, presenting the shooting as a curiosity of a bullet that went "straight to his heart" and wounded a second man.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Oscar Fifer
bases: A crowd of Black residents surrounded the jail holding Fifer after he killed Whiteside and said they would lynch him before morning, a threatened lynching (A1, A2).

No one was reported killed by the crowd; the only death was Whiteside's in the quarrel, and the coverage does not report what became of the threat against Fifer (A1, A2, A3). The crowd's stated aim of lynching a jailed man for a killing was an extralegal punishment under the pretext of justice, but it was not reported carried out.
The jail siege and lynching threat appear only in one Chattanooga wire (A1, A2); the shooting itself is corroborated by an independent news-brief paragraph (A3) that does not mention the threat.

accounts.label: Chattanooga wire
accounts.gist: Fifer and Whiteside renewed an old quarrel; Whiteside assaulted Fifer with a knife and Fifer shot him dead; Negroes surrounded the jail and said they would lynch Fifer before morning.

accounts.label: News-brief paragraph
accounts.gist: In a quarrel Fifer fired at Whiteside; the bullet passed through Whiteside's heart and seriously wounded a bystander named Brown fifty feet away. It says nothing of who began the fight or of the jail.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch ran the wire as 'Fatal Affray in Tennessee', labeling Fifer 'white' and Whiteside 'mulatto' and giving the knife assault as fact.
The Savannah Morning News put the Black crowd in its headline, 'Negroes Surround a Jail', over the same wire text.
The news-brief paragraph treated the shooting as a curiosity of the bullet's flight, without races or the jail.

conflicts.note: The two printings of the same wire differ; the independent brief paragraph agrees with 'heart'.
